Introduction

The industrial revolution had a massive impact on the growth of towns. In 1700 Manchester was a small village with less than 10,000 inhabitants. By 1801 Greater Manchester had become a city of 328,609 people. Liverpool, Leeds and Huddersfield were similar in size. By 1851 the population of Manchester had increased to 1,037,001 and the north of England contained half the population of the country. London too had grown from of a population of 1,011,157 in 1801 to 2,651,939 in 1851 and by 5,571,968 by 1891.

People came to the towns in search of work. The development of steam power meant that factories did not have to be located near rivers using water for power. Factories offered higher wages than agricultural work. Their workforce was often forced to live in crowded back-to-back housing, built by factory owners near to the factory. Rows of houses were separated from each other by a court, or strip of muddy ground. There were no bathrooms, toilets, running water or heating apart from a single fireplace also used for cooking. People would have to share a water pump and privy in the street which probably served at least twenty houses. The privies often overflowed and the waste often soaked into wells that supplied the water pump, or flooded into the court which was turned into an open sewer running between the houses. These cramped houses were often home to four or five families, possibly with lodgers and another family living in the cellar. The cellars themselves were damp, dark and frequently subject to flooding.

Extracts in this collection from the 'Second Report of Commissioners of Inquiry into the State of Large Towns and Populous. Districts, 1842' [HO 45/416] for example, describe conditions in Birmingham, Hull, Manchester, Liverpool Sunderland, Aberdeen and Edinburgh. The extracts also provide some insight into the work of the commission, how it gathered its evidence and made recommendations. Taken with several 'nuisance letters' from private individuals to the General Board of Health about a range of different 'nuisances'- piles of rubbish and waste, poor drains or sewers or livestock in the streets or effects of a nearby gasworks for example, [MH13/261] we get a graphic insight into living conditions in the towns.

Unsurprisingly, the average life expectancy contrasted greatly between town and countryside and also shows a great disparity between social classes. In 1840, 57% of the poor children living in Manchester died before they were 5 years. In rural areas this was 32%. An agricultural worker in Rutland had a life-expectancy of 38, a factory worker in Liverpool, a life expectancy of 15 years. Urban living was not conducive to good health for the poorer classes particularly and cholera thrived in situations where there was an impure water supply. Documents here also explore the response to cholera from quack cures, like the cholera bath [MH 13/245/120] or use of brandy, [HO 44/25] to government advice in 1831 [HO 44/24/57] capturing the palpable fear with which this disease was held.

The layout of an industrial town reflected its class divisions. The poorest lived in the central slums near the factories. Extracts from a report [HO 44/24/87] sent to the Home Office from by the Medical Secretary for Visiting District Committees of the local Board of Health for St Margaret and St John the Evangelist also provide a picture of living conditions in Westminster in 1831 for example. Surrounding the centre of city, skilled trades' people lived in small terraced houses. Moving further away, the middle classes built their semi-detached villas in Turnham Green like the design shown [COPY 1.39 f348] in this collection. Larger detached homes with running water and large gardens existed in the more rural suburbs, and may have had the look of the 'country house' in the cut out source. [COPY 1/ 59 f258]. These homes later became more comfortable as they were supplied with electricity, [ZPER 35/9].

The rapid growth of towns meant there was little attention to urban planning including proper sewage and drainage systems or decent paving. Rubbish and filth accumulated in the streets, there was no systematic rubbish collection or street cleaning. There was no fire service, this was left to private companies. There was no control over air pollution either, so factory smoke and smog were a regular fact of life. London, and the cities in the midlands and north of the country were the unhealthiest places to live. Disease spread rapidly, especially among the urban poor. Cholera, smallpox and typhoid were common causes of death. Public health improved in the city of London with the achievement of Joseph Bazalgette, an engineer who built a sewer network for London in the 1870s. This was crucial in reducing cholera epidemics as it prevented raw sewage being emptied into the Thames.

I now have enough grounded material to sketch a balanced framing for the exhibit. Here is how I'd advise structuring the narrative.

Begin the exhibit by naming the trap directly: historians themselves split into "optimists," who point to rising real wages and note that child labor and rural hardship predated factories, and "pessimists," who weigh hours, infant mortality, and lost political rights more heavily, and neither camp has settled the argument with the surviving wage and mortality data. [shard_02727_52308] [shard_02363_75995]

That framing lets you tell visitors up front that both "machines made life better" and "factories were hell" are real historical arguments, not settled facts, and the exhibit's job is to show why intelligent people still disagree.

For migration, ground the scale in numbers: London grew from about 675,000 people in 1750 to roughly four million by 1880, and by 1851 over three-quarters of Manchester's adults had been born elsewhere, having left villages for mill towns like Leeds and Manchester once wage work no longer required staying tied to land. [shard_01083_57525]

Manchester itself ballooned from a village of under 10,000 around 1700 to over a million people by 1851, and steam power let factories locate away from rivers entirely, pulling migrants toward wages rather than water-power sites. [shard_04285_37025]

On living conditions, be concrete rather than abstract: newcomers were squeezed into back-to-back terraces with shared taps and privies, no running water, and cellars prone to flooding, and Edwin Chadwick's 1842 sanitary investigations and 1848 report tied this squalor directly to disease and to the class divide between the governing classes who never saw it and the workers who lived it. [shard_01116_65787]

The mortality gap makes the stakes tangible for families and students alike: in 1840, 57 percent of poor children in Manchester died before age five versus 32 percent in rural areas, and a Liverpool factory worker's life expectancy was about 15 years against 38 for an agricultural worker in Rutland. [shard_04285_37025]

Friedrich Engels's 1844 account of Manchester's shanty-like courts is the classic pessimist document, but by his own 1892 introduction he noted many of those conditions had since improved, especially after the 1875 Public Health Act encouraged more sanitary "byelaw" terraced housing. [shard_03641_37935]

For children and work, lay out both the ordinary cruelty and the changing law side by side: children as young as four or five worked in mills and mines through the early 1800s, and Parliament responded in stages — the 1833 Factory Act barred children under nine and limited hours for young persons, the 1842 Mines Act (championed by Lord Ashley, later Earl of Shaftesbury, after his Children's Employment Commission exposed conditions) removed women and children from underground work, and the 1847 Ten Hours Act capped the working day, with schooling requirements and further extensions following into the 1870s. [shard_01977_57270] [shard_05460_81767]

The 1833 act specifically limited children under eleven to nine hours a day and young persons under eighteen to twelve, added factory inspectors, and by 1844 extended hour limits to adult women and introduced half-time schooling for child workers, so the law visibly reshaped the shop floor rather than just condemning it on paper. [shard_05355_10363]

On women's work, resist a simple loss-of-status story: industrialization did separate home from workplace and pulled many women into "cheap" factory or outwork labor, but the mid-Victorian domestic ideology that treated a working wife as improper spread across classes precisely because paid work outside the home, not work itself, was the objection, and most working-class women who took paid work did so for survival and stopped once the crisis passed. [shard_01738_19991]

That same domestic ideal coexisted with real female political activity — women signed antislavery petitions in the hundreds of thousands by 1833, formed Female Reform Societies, and made up roughly a quarter of the Peterloo Massacre casualties in 1819 — so "separate spheres" was never the whole story of women's public life. [shard_05285_5335]

On class and family, offer the exhibit a genuine scholarly debate rather than a slogan: sociologist Talcott Parsons argued industrialization broke up large extended households into isolated nuclear families, but historian Peter Laslett's research found only about 10 percent of English households before 1821 already contained extended kin, suggesting the small nuclear family may have preceded, not resulted from, industrialization. [shard_03159_54814]

Not every employer fit the "dark satanic mill" image either: paternalist industrialists such as Robert Owen at New Lanark, Titus Salt at Saltaire, and the Cadbury and Lever families built model villages with decent housing for their workers, even as most factory owners resisted the very hour limits that Parliament kept expanding through 1874. [shard_01546_24460]

For labor politics, Chartism deserves real space as the era's central working-class political project: the People's Charter of 1838 demanded universal manhood suffrage, secret ballots, and payment of MPs, gathered petitions signed by over a million and later over three million people, and was rejected each time by Parliament, yet nearly every one of its six points except annual parliaments was eventually enacted piecemeal in later decades. [shard_02400_8902]

That arc connects backward to the Combination Acts that outlawed unions after the French Revolution, the 1819 Peterloo Massacre of protesting cotton workers, and the 1824 repeal of the Combination Acts, and forward through the Reform Acts of 1832, 1867, and 1884 to the eventual founding of the Labour Party — a century-long widening of political voice running alongside industrial change. [shard_04615_35829]

Finally, on later reforms, show visitors that "the picture changed" concretely rather than assert it: the 1870 Forster's Act created state-funded schools and the 1880 Act made attendance compulsory, effectively phasing out the youngest child laborers by replacing their factory hours with classroom hours. [shard_01138_76863]

The 1875 Public Health Act, passed under Disraeli partly under pressure from mass suffrage protests and rising working-class organization, required running water and drainage in new housing and let local authorities begin clearing slums — a reform explicitly framed at the time as improving conditions for "the masses," not charity for the poor. [shard_03390_18709]

A single closing timeline for the exhibit wall could run: 1832 Reform Act, 1833 Factory Act, 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act, 1838–48 Chartism, 1847 Ten Hours Act, 1846 Corn Law repeal, 1870 Education Act, 1875 Public Health Act — a chain of political fights, not a single dial that flipped from misery to progress. [shard_05257_40283]

The honest frame for families and school groups, then, is neither triumph nor tragedy but contest: real wages and life expectancy improved unevenly and late, reform came only after decades of protest, petition, and disaster, and the "better life" many visitors associate with industrial Britain was won through the very struggles the exhibit should put front and center, not delivered automatically by the machines themselves.
